#4976. Nvidia, AMD, Micron Sink as Anthropic Closes 17% Above IPO Price

Nvidia, AMD, Micron Sink as Anthropic Closes 17% Above IPO Price

Anthropic made stock market history Thursday, raising $81.34 billion in the largest initial IPO share sale ever. But Wall Street's response was considerably less enthusiastic than the demand for the Claude developer's shares.

The stock opened at $111.50 on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, a 34% premium over its $83 offering price, briefly pushing the company's fully diluted valuation past $2 trillion.

The rally faded quickly, however, with shares dropping toward $93 before closing today at $97.17.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The offering involved 980 million shares and surpassed SpaceX's original $75 billion IPO in June. As Decrypt previously reported, SpaceX's expanded final offering reached $86.25 billion, meaning Anthropic has not surpassed that completed deal.

Investors initially welcomed the listing, sending technology stocks higher before the opening bell. By the afternoon, however, the Nasdaq Composite was down 2.06%, the S&P 500 had fallen 1.9%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was off 2.17%.

The selloff extended across the AI supply chain. A Thursday afternoon market heatmap showed Nvidia falling 3.4%, Broadcom losing 2.07%, and memory chipmaker Micron slipping 2.17%. Microsoft was down 1.97%, while cloud infrastructure and software provider Oracle declined 2.97%.

AMD was among the hardest hit, down 7.73% in the day, although its decline had a separate catalyst. Reuters reported that the chipmaker came under pressure after investigative outlet Hunterbrook disclosed that its affiliated investment fund had taken a short position in the company.

The picture was not uniformly negative. Palo Alto Networks rose 6%, CrowdStrike gained 2.24%, and Intel added 2.25% in the same snapshot. The divergence shows that investors were distinguishing between companies rather than selling every technology stock indiscriminately.

The broader weakness comes as investors question the cost of building AI infrastructure and the returns companies can generate from that spending. Nvidia's latest earnings beat expectations, but uncertainty following Jensen Huang's resignation has continued to weigh on the semiconductor giant.

Anthropic also faces an expensive expansion. Its IPO disclosures detailed approximately $900.9 billion in infrastructure and computing commitments extending through 2045, alongside another $150 billion to $175 billion in estimated payments under less precisely defined arrangements.

"Anthropic's record-breaking IPO has failed to rekindle enthusiasm for tech stocks," Joe Maher, market economist at Capital Economics, told Reuters.

Nvidia's weakness was notable given its latest results. The chipmaker reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue on Tuesday, up 103% from a year earlier, and forecast stronger-than-expected sales for the following quarter.

Even those numbers failed to erase concerns over the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang after allegations of extramarital affairs and possible leaks of corporate secrets and the sustainability of the AI spending boom.

The pressure also reached companies that rent out computing capacity. Neocloud operators CoreWeave and Nebius fell 5.0% and 7.8%, respectively. Software companies were weak as well: Salesforce declined 3.17% and Adobe lost 2.03% in the afternoon heatmap. From chips and data centers to enterprise software, the losses extended beyond any single corner of the AI trade.

Anthropic's IPO prospectus shows how closely these companies are tied together. Nvidia and Google each committed roughly $10 billion to a conditional private share placement alongside the IPO.

AMD agreed to invest $2.5 billion; Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft committed $1 billion apiece; and TSMC pledged $500 million. The $26 billion placement is separate from the public offering. Several of these investors are also key suppliers or infrastructure partners in the AI ecosystem.

That creates a central question for investors: How much of the money flowing into AI companies will ultimately translate into profitable demand for chips, cloud capacity and software?

Anthropic's blockbuster debut demonstrates demand for its shares, but Thursday's broader decline shows that Wall Street is not ready to extend that confidence to every company financing or supplying the AI boom.

#4975. Strategy raises its buyback ceiling to $4 billion as MSTR shares sink 21%

The company has spent nearly $2.9 billion retiring preferred shares, while analysts question the economics of funding those purchases with common-stock issuance.

Strategy raised its STRC buyback authorization for the third time on Monday, bringing the program to $4 billion as its common shares continued to struggle.

The Bitcoin treasury company had exhausted nearly $2.88 billion, or nearly 96% of its previous $3 billion authorization, after spending another $211.8 million repurchasing STRC during the week ended Nov. 22.

The latest expansion comes as Strategy's common shares have fallen 21.1% since it announced its first STRC repurchases on July 27. MSTR closed at $77.80 on Nov. 20, compared with $98.65 nearly four months earlier.

Strategy launched its initial $1 billion digital credit repurchase program in June, then increased it to $2 billion in September and $3 billion in October. Monday's announcement marks the third consecutive $1 billion expansion, bringing cumulative expansion to $4 billion.

The growing commitment has coincided with a shift in how Strategy deploys money raised from common shareholders.

According to its latest SEC filing, the company issued 1.93 million MSTR shares last week, raising $176.7 million.

Of those proceeds, $147 million (83.2%) funded STRC repurchases, while only $29.6 million (16.8%) went toward acquiring 457 Bitcoin.

Strategy contributed another $64.8 million from existing cash to complete the $211.8 million preferred-share repurchase.

Weekly repurchase spending in US dollars, reported amounts are rounded to $0.1M.

Source: Strategy Form 8-K, Nov. 23, 2026 · STRC Live historical buyback ledger

The spending has helped reduce its future dividend obligations but has not kept STRC consistently near its $100 stated amount. The security closed at $93.60 on Nov. 20, despite Strategy maintaining a 12% annual dividend rate to support its price.

Meanwhile, Strategy retains a separate $1 billion authorization to repurchase MSTR shares, which remained entirely unused last week.

Bitcoin analyst Derin Olenik criticized the continued issuance of common shares to finance preferred-share repurchases, arguing the transactions weaken shareholders' underlying Bitcoin exposure.

Strategy's published figures support a decline in gross Bitcoin holdings per assumed diluted share during the latest reporting week.

Its outstanding Bitcoin balance increased from 850,849 BTC on Nov. 15 to 851,305 BTC on Nov. 22, while assumed diluted shares outstanding rose from approximately 457.24 million to 459.19 million.

Consequently, gross Bitcoin per share declined from approximately 186,082 satoshis to 185,392 satoshis, a reduction of about 690 satoshis (0.37%).

However, Strategy executive chairman Michael Saylor defended the transactions, arguing that Strategy's approach has consistently increased shareholders' net Bitcoin exposure despite the dilution.

“Our trades accreted Net BPS in each of the last 13 weeks. Cumulatively, we increased Net BPS by 584 sats/share and generated a Net BTC Gain of 2,505 BTC or $199M before preferred dividends, measured at a fixed $BTC price each week.”

Strategy-reported positive weekly contributions to net BTC per common share (in satoshis) before preferred dividends and holding BTC price fixed within each week. Values are transcribed from the supplied Strategy-branded Nov. 23 chart at one-decimal precision.

Source: Strategy net BPS methodology; individual values from supplied Strategy-branded chart · Strategy, November 23, 2026 corporate disclosure · Strategy, November 19 commentary on previous 12 weeks

Saylor also reported that the latest week's transactions increased Net Bitcoin Per Share by six satoshis and improved Strategy's Net Reserve by $183 million.

The conflicting figures reflect competing assessments of Strategy's capital allocation. Gross Bitcoin per share measures its holdings against diluted shares, while Strategy's Net Bitcoin Per Share accounts for senior claims and dollar assets when calculating the Bitcoin exposure attributable to common shareholders.

Under Saylor's framework, retiring preferred securities can increase net exposure even when common-share issuance reduces gross Bitcoin holdings per share.

Olenik remained critical of the economics, questioning whether the increasingly complex transactions justify the continued dilution of common shareholders.

He also challenged the economics of STRC repurchases. His calculations put the security's average issuance price at $95.81 and its average repurchase price at $97.93, meaning Strategy has spent more buying back preferred shares than it originally received per share issued.

Average price estimated by dividing reported weekly spending, rounded to $0.1M, by shares repurchased. Per-share cents are approximate.

Source: Strategy Form 8-K, Nov. 23, 2026 · STRC Live historical buyback ledger

Strategy has defended repurchases below STRC's $100 stated amount because retiring the securities reduces future dividend obligations.

Saylor said Strategy has reduced outstanding credit by $2.9 billion in recent months, lowering annual dividend obligations by approximately $353 million.

The latest transactions alone retired 2.18 million STRC shares, eliminating approximately $26.2 million in annualized dividends at the current 12% rate.

However, the company's latest decision suggests that reducing those obligations will remain a major capital priority.

Alongside the third buyback expansion, Strategy authorized transferring $1 billion from its dedicated USD Reserve into discretionary USD Cash, which management can use for further repurchases or Bitcoin purchases.

The change marks a departure from its original July policy, which explicitly prohibited using the USD Reserve to fund STRC repurchases.

Saylor said the reallocation was possible because the company's remaining reserve could cover its dividend and interest obligations for 3.4 years.

Following the adjustment, Strategy reported approximately $3.7 billion in dedicated reserves and over $1 billion in discretionary cash, leaving total dollar assets at roughly $4.8 billion.

Olenik interpreted the move as evidence that Strategy was preparing to rely more heavily on existing liquidity when issuing MSTR shares becomes less attractive.

That would let Strategy continue retiring preferred securities without relying entirely on new common-share issuance, although the company has not committed the reallocated cash to a specific purchase.

Strategy now has $1.1 billion in remaining preferred-share buyback authority, nearly matching its discretionary cash balance.

Its next capital-allocation decision will determine whether the expanded financial resources support further STRC repurchases or reverse the recent pattern of relatively modest Bitcoin purchases and continued MSTR dilution.

Bitcoin fell to a cycle low near $55,100 over the weekend amid continued risk-off sentiment, macro headwinds, and an AI equities-led stock market downturn.

Spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds in the U.S. reported around $1.79 billion in net outflows last week, the largest weekly withdrawal since the week ended June 26, 2026.

This marked the fourth consecutive week of outflows for the funds, according to data from SoSoValue. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) led the outflows with $1.37 billion alone during the week.

So far this month, around $4.14 billion has left bitcoin ETFs, trailing June's record monthly net outflows. Total net assets in the bitcoin ETFs sat at $71.35 billion as of Friday, down from around $110 billion in mid-September.

Spot ether Ethereum (ETH) ETFs also reported $314 million in weekly outflows, making it the eighth consecutive week of negative flows.

Laevitas Head of Markets Rick Maeda told The Block that the current net outflow represents "mostly risk reduction" among investors. "Profit-taking usually follows a rally, but these outflows have come into a falling market, with BTC sliding from around $80,000 at the start of the month to the low $60,000s," said Maeda.

Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) fell to a cycle low near $55,700 over the weekend amid continued risk-off sentiment, macro headwinds, and an AI equities-led stock market downturn. The Nasdaq Composite fell around 10% last week, and the S&P 500 dropped 8.6% as the scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang fueled wider concerns about the sustainability of the AI sector. Dan Khus, chief analyst at LVRG Research, said the current ETF outflow streak appears to be more structural than previous outflows.

"Unlike earlier outflow periods that were often shorter and more reactive to single events, the current four-week streak appears more structural, coinciding with sustained price pressure, elevated liquidations, and a shift in institutional positioning toward capital preservation," Khus commented.

Risk-averse investors are moving further away from crypto products as they expect the Federal Reserve to deliver another interest rate hike in December, analysts said. The U.S. Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, scheduled to be announced this Wednesday, may hint at how sticky inflation remains, and whether the Federal Reserve will proceed with another rate hike in December, BTSE COO Jeff Mei said.

"Bitcoin and ether ETFs may face further outflows as rate-hike concerns and weak risk appetite weigh on institutional demand," Zeus Research Analyst Dominick John said. "Bitcoin is likely to remain more resilient, while Ether faces greater pressure. A sustained recovery will depend on easing macro fears and renewed inflows."

#4972. Bitcoin’s supply squeeze narrative faces scrutiny after 11,000 BTC moves to Kraken

Coinbase and Binance sent large amounts of Bitcoin to Kraken during the downturn, even as combined exchange reserves declined.

More than 11,000 BTC moved from Coinbase and Binance to Kraken during Saturday's selloff, complicating Bitcoin's supply-squeeze narrative.

The five transactions, identified by Ask The Tape (ATT), came as major exchanges recorded hundreds of millions of dollars in net Bitcoin withdrawals, fueling expectations that fewer coins were available for trading.

However, the transfers revealed substantial movements between trading venues, with Bitcoin leaving some exchanges only to replenish reserves elsewhere.

Coinbase accounted for approximately 4,028 BTC across two transactions. The first delivered 2,177.79 BTC to Kraken-tagged addresses at 03:47 UTC, followed by another 1,850 BTC at 10:04 UTC.

Binance then transferred 7,000 BTC through three transactions: two transfers of 2,000 BTC each and a third involving 3,000 BTC.

The movements coincided with substantial differences in exchange flows reported by CryptoQuant.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Binance recorded $680 million in net Bitcoin withdrawals on Nov. 21, while Coinbase and Bybit registered $373 million and $103 million, respectively. Together, the three exchanges lost approximately $1.16 billion.

Kraken moved in the opposite direction, receiving $478 million in net inflows and offsetting 41% of those withdrawals.

That left the four platforms with a combined net outflow of $678 million, even as substantial amounts of Bitcoin circulated between their wallets.

Kraken also recorded significant outgoing transactions that day, including one involving approximately 4,028 BTC, illustrating the rapid movement of liquidity across exchanges during the downturn.

The exchange movements have become particularly significant as Bitcoin struggles to recover from its recent decline below $60,000.

Although declining exchange reserves can reduce the amount of Bitcoin immediately available for sale, sustained buying demand remains essential to turning that scarcity into upward price pressure.

That demand has weakened considerably among US institutional investors.

According to Farside Investors, US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.7 billion in net withdrawals last week, extending a period of heavy redemptions that has stripped billions of dollars from the funds this month.

While Bitcoin subsequently recovered above $61,000 on Nov. 23, the ETF withdrawals have yet to show a corresponding recovery in institutional appetite.

The next test arrives Wednesday, when the US Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes October's personal consumption expenditures inflation report alongside its second estimate of third-quarter economic growth.

Both releases are scheduled for 8:30 a.m. ET and could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve's December interest rate decision.

Stronger inflation could push Treasury yields and the dollar higher, adding pressure to Bitcoin at a time when ETF investors are withdrawing capital.

That leaves Bitcoin's recovery dependent on two developments: exchange reserves continuing to decline across trading venues and fresh buying demand returning to absorb available supply.

If ETF withdrawals persist while Bitcoin continues circulating between exchanges, the apparent supply squeeze may offer little support against another wave of selling.

#4971. ECB seeks industry partners for tokenized deposits, securities experiments

Industry groups have until Dec. 11 to apply for the ECB’s first experimental exercises under its Appia initiative, with later submissions reviewed on a rolling basis.

The European Central Bank (ECB) is seeking financial market participants to help explore tokenized deposits and securities as part of its efforts to build an integrated European financial ecosystem using blockchain technology.

On Friday, the ECB invited industry groups to participate in analytical work and experiments under its Appia initiative, identifying three priority areas, including tokenized deposits and related payments, tokenized securities and shared network governance.

According to the ECB, interested participants must apply as part of a collective initiative comprising independent legal entities rather than individually. Groups can apply for one or more workstreams, with proposals evaluated based on factors including expertise, practical experience, technical readiness and expected contributions.

Applications for the first experimental exercises are due by Dec. 11, while later submissions will be assessed on a rolling basis.

The initiative builds on the Eurosystem’s broader Appia roadmap, which aims to develop a unified European tokenized financial ecosystem anchored in central bank money. The ECB plans to publish a blueprint outlining findings and a proposed framework in 2028.

The invitation comes as ECB President Christine Lagarde warned that Europe risks missing an opportunity to establish an integrated market for tokenized securities if incompatible standards emerge across platforms.

Lagarde urged policymakers to establish common rules to prevent fragmentation as blockchain-based financial infrastructure develops across the region.

#4970. Citi Says Customers Are Responsible When AI Banking Agents Go Rogue—Even After a Hack

Citi Says Customers Are Responsible When AI Banking Agents Go Rogue—Even After a Hack

Citi has updated its online banking terms to make customers responsible for the actions of third-party AI agents accessing their accounts, including when an agent leaks their credentials and someone else uses them to get in.

The change, reported by TechCrunch Wednesday, makes explicit how the bank intends to handle an increasingly awkward question: Who pays when software handling your money makes a mistake?

Under Citi’s new terms, actions taken using credentials supplied to an outside agent are treated as authorized by the customer, even if the tool ignores instructions, exceeds its permissions, or shares those credentials with another party.

Citi says it has no obligation to investigate whether the agent followed the customer's original prompts, subject to applicable law.

A Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch that the November revision clarifies the risks of sharing banking credentials or granting outside tools account access. The provision does not apply to AI agents offered by Citi itself.

Citi is not acting alone. JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies in October, while Citizens Bank warned customers this week by email that they could be responsible for what their AI assistants do.

PNC also changed its digital agreement on Wednesday. Its rules distinguish bank-approved connections, which can provide limited access, from handing an agent unrestricted access to an account.

The move follows a banking security scare from October 22. Major banks had detected AI agents logging into customer accounts, sometimes taking steps that appeared to go beyond their users' instructions, and executives said they struggled to determine which agents had been properly authorized.

An AI agent differs from a conventional chatbot because it can act on a user's behalf, potentially navigating websites, accessing financial records, or initiating payments. That makes a mistaken instruction or compromised login more consequential than a bad answer about a bank balance.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency has since issued AI examiner guidance that addresses outside agents, payment controls, and human approval. The framework is nonbinding and does not itself create new requirements for banks.

Citi's language does not automatically eliminate consumer fraud protections. Under U.S. federal consumer protection rules, banks generally must investigate unauthorized electronic transfers and limit customers' financial liability for fraud. Those protections cannot simply be waived through a banking agreement, although their application to transactions performed by customer-authorized AI agents remains less clear.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says banks cannot use agreements to waive those legal protections, although the rules distinguish theft by an outsider from transfers actually authorized by a customer or someone given access.

Whether a particular AI-related loss qualifies as unauthorized depends on how the transaction occurred.

PNC's updated agreement takes a stricter operational approach: Customers may use certain connection methods approved by the bank, but cannot give third-party AI agents their passwords or one-time security codes, and agents generally cannot initiate payments unless PNC expressly permits it.

#4969. Singapore’s OCBC, StraitsX launch pilot for cross-border business stablecoin payments

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The setup uses StraitsX's infrastructure for onchain collection and compliance, while OCBC handles the fiat off-ramp.

OCBC, a major bank in Singapore, has launched a pilot with StraitsX for cross-border business-to-business stablecoin payments.

In a statement released Monday, StraitsX wrote that the trial connects stablecoin settlement with participating OCBC clients' existing bank accounts. The setup uses StraitsX's "Dedicated Wallet Address" infrastructure for onchain collection and compliance, while OCBC handles the fiat off-ramp process.

The pilot is designed to explore how businesses can receive cross-border payments through their existing OCBC bank accounts without directly managing the underlying stablecoins, according to the statement. The pair said they will initially test selected cross-border payment flows.

NTT DOCOMO Asia, a Singapore entity of Japanese mobile carrier NTT DOCOMO, is the first customer participating in the trial.

"As new forms of digital money emerge, businesses are looking for ways to harness their benefits without adding complexity to their day-to-day financial operations," Carmen Chan, deputy head of global transaction banking at OCBC, said in the statement. "Our collaboration with StraitsX allows us to explore how stablecoin-based payments can be integrated with established banking services, while keeping the customer experience seamless."

The latest stablecoin effort came after OCBC, StraitsX, and Standard Chartered announced last week a proof-of-concept that explores interoperability between tokenized deposit networks issued by different banks.

StraitsX, which holds a Major Payment Institution license under the Monetary Authority of Singapore, offers a stablecoin-native settlement layer for global finance. It also issues the XSGD and XUSD stablecoins. OCBC, meanwhile, is the second-largest financial services group in Southeast Asia by assets.

The latest pilot comes as Singapore's financial institutions and crypto players step up efforts to expand the use of tokenized assets. Both OCBC and StraitsX participate in the BLOOM initiative, which the Monetary Authority of Singapore launched in October 2025 to develop use cases for tokenized bank deposits and stablecoins.

The MAS also said last week that it issued S$100 million ($77.5 million) of four-week tokenized MAS Bills on Nov. 6 through its Singapore Dollar Test Network. The bills were settled in wholesale CBDC.

Also last week, DBS Bank and Kinexys by JPMorgan announced an interoperability solution that allows institutions to make 24/7 transfers of tokenized deposits between the U.S. and Singapore.

#4968. Cross River Bank Launches Its First Bitcoin-Backed Loans With LendingUSA

Cross River Bank has launched its first bitcoin-backed loans, working with consumer lender LendingUSA to let eligible borrowers take out between $10,000 and $250,000 against their BTC without selling it.

The program is the first time Cross River has originated bitcoin-secured loans itself, according to The Block. LendingUSA runs the application platform, and every loan is made by Cross River, a New Jersey state-chartered bank, according to LendingUSA.

Borrowers can choose a loan-to-value ratio of 30%, 50% or 70%, which sets how much cash they receive against the value of the bitcoin they pledge. LendingUSA defines the ratio as the loan balance divided by the value of the collateral, so a 50% loan against $100,000 of bitcoin would be $50,000. Two repayment options are offered: interest-only or no monthly payments.

On an interest-only loan, borrowers make smaller monthly payments that roughly cover interest, with the principal and any remaining interest due at the end of the term. On a no-monthly-payment loan, the full balance plus interest is due at the end. LendingUSA says borrowers can repay early without penalties or fees.

Applicants go through a soft credit check, and LendingUSA says approval rests on the crypto being pledged rather than a credit score. The company says funding typically arrives within one to three business days after the collateral is verified.

A qualified third-party custodian holds the bitcoin for the life of the loan. Once the loan is repaid in full, the collateral is released back to the borrower, according to the company.

The terms carry the usual risk of borrowing against a volatile asset. LendingUSA says that if the value of the bitcoin falls, the loan-to-value ratio rises, and borrowers may be asked to add collateral or pay down the debt to avoid liquidation. The company says it will try to notify borrowers first but cannot guarantee it during fast price moves.

The timing matters. Bitcoin was trading near $61,000 on Monday morning, so a borrower at the 70% tier would have far less room before a collateral call than one at the 30% tier. Lower ratios leave a bigger cushion but unlock less cash per bitcoin pledged.

LendingUSA markets the loans for uses such as debt consolidation, home improvements and large purchases. The company says it has served more than 200,000 borrowers across its lending business, and the crypto product is its first expansion into digital asset-backed loans.

Cross River President Evan Russo framed the launch as a natural extension of the bank’s work. “Digital assets have become a meaningful part of how many consumers build and hold wealth, and the financial system must evolve to serve them responsibly,” Russo said in a statement.

“Cross River was built on the belief that innovation and trusted infrastructure go hand in hand,” he added. “Launching our first Bitcoin-secured lending program as the loan originator is a natural extension of that mission.”

The move adds a state-chartered bank to a lending market that has been moving closer to traditional finance. In August, Coinbase and Better Mortgage announced general availability of bitcoin-backed mortgages, and in April, Strike’s Jack Mallers announced lending proof-of-reserves and loans designed to withstand volatility.

Neither company has said how much bitcoin has been pledged so far or which custodian holds the collateral. LendingUSA’s page says rates and terms vary by applicant, and that loan amounts, interest rates and terms are disclosed once an application is received.

For now, the page lists the product’s maximum loan-to-value at 70%, and every loan on it is made by Cross River Bank.

#4967. GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 expose a blind spot in AI oversight

In a METR exercise, Opus 5.5 scored GPT-6 Astra’s proposed AI tests about 0.2 points higher on a 0–1 scale than a human scorer did. A gap that large could affect which tests get pursued.

In METR’s test of AI oversight, Opus 5.5 gave GPT-6 Astra’s proposed AI tests higher scores than the human evaluator did. METR said the gap could change whether its scoring rules recommended pursuing a test. In a separate exercise, leading AI agents placed ahead of most human entrants across 15 past programming contests.

Across Al Zimmermann’s programming contests, METR reported median placements from the 96th to the 98th percentile for Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. About four people still beat the strongest models in the median contest.

The agents had 48 hours per contest on a 28-core machine. Each submission gave them a numerical score they could use to see whether their changes improved the result. Human contestants typically had about three calendar months, used their own hardware and could see the public standings. METR compared the agents’ scores with the original contest results.

In a separate exercise, METR asked agents to design tests that would help researchers assess what AI models could do. AI judges and a human scorer had access to project files, scores from trial runs and the agents’ case for why their tests were relevant and feasible. The human scorer assessed whether each proposed test was worth including in METR’s suite. METR said none of the designs was useful enough to include in its report.

The AI judges tended to agree more closely with the human scorer when a weaker model had designed the test. When the model that designed the test was as capable as the judge or stronger, the judges tended to rate the work more highly than the human did. Opus 5.5 agreed most closely with the human scorer, yet rated GPT-6 Astra’s proposals about 0.2 points higher on average on a scale from zero to one.

The comparison came from one exercise, and what counted as useful depended in part on METR’s research priorities. METR said models underused some resources in the judgment tests. It also reported strong model performance on some longer machine-learning tasks with automatic scoring. A separate AI peer review audit tested whether reviewers’ objections changed the findings by running code on the underlying data.

#4966. CryptoUK Urges FCA Not to Treat DeFi Devs as Regulated by Default

CryptoUK Urges FCA Not to Treat DeFi Devs as Regulated by Default

The UK's main crypto trade association has called on the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) to make sure that developers and governance participants in decentralized finance protocols are not treated as regulated firms by default.

CryptoUK set out its position in a response to the FCA's consultation paper CP26/36, which proposes guidance on the "perimeter" of the UK's new crypto regime: which activities fall inside it and need FCA authorization, and which don't. The group, which says it represents more than 150 crypto companies, submitted its response on Wednesday, November 18, the day the consultation closed, and published it a day later.

Yesterday, CryptoUK submitted its response to the Financial Conduct Authority’s Consultation Paper CP26/36, which proposes amendments to the Perimeter Guidance Manual (PERG) to reflect the FSMA 2000 (Cryptoassets) (Miscellaneous Amendments) Regulations 2026.

The consultation… pic.twitter.com/oOrZgAWscP

— CryptoUK (@CryptoUKAssoc) November 19, 2026

"Software development, maintenance, security work and participation in decentralised governance should not, by themselves, establish that a person carries on a regulated activity," CryptoUK wrote. That would be consistent with the FCA's "clear controlling person" approach to DeFi, under which regulation should hinge on who effectively controls a financial service, it argued.

CryptoUK said it "broadly" supports the draft guidance, which reflects further amendments to the UK's crypto legislation that the government laid in September. The FCA aims to publish its final guidance in January 2027. It welcomed new exclusions from the regime for temporary settlement and payment arrangements, assets backing UK-recognized stablecoins, proprietary trading and market making, and technical service providers.

But in several places, the draft "goes further than the legislation," the group said. It pointed to a proposed link to the UK based on where a protocol is developed or governed, requirements in the exclusions for payments and proprietary trading, and indicators that would narrow the exclusion for technical services. The FCA has acknowledged that the timing of the latest amendments created uncertainty for some firms, and said it will give applicants extra time where questions over the technical services exclusion held up their applications for authorization.

The group asked the FCA to publish a public record of stablecoins that qualify under the UK regime, to clarify how stablecoins differ from electronic money, and to include more examples of activities that typically fall outside the perimeter.

CryptoUK also urged the FCA to raise with the Treasury outcomes that put UK firms at a disadvantage, citing the treatment of UK technical providers that offer access to regulated overseas trading venues, and of payments using stablecoins issued abroad. The UK should align with the EU's MiCA framework "where appropriate," it said. The response was prepared with law firm CMS and signed by CryptoUK policy director Nick Brooks.

The consultation is part of the FCA's work to build out the UK's crypto rulebook. The regulator finalized its core rules for crypto firms in June, ahead of a regime due to take effect on October 25, 2027, and later issued guidance two weeks before its authorization window for crypto firms opened. It has also set out a shared vision for tokenization with the Bank of England.

#4965. South Korea to publish draft of comprehensive crypto legal framework this week

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The draft is expected to include a licensing regime for crypto businesses and a bank-centered issuance system for local stablecoins.

South Korea's Financial Services Commission is preparing to release the government's draft for the Digital Asset Basic Act later this week, according to multiple local news reports.

The act is expected to become the country's second major piece of crypto legislation following the Virtual Asset User Protection Act, which took effect in 2024. While that earlier legislation focused primarily on protecting user assets and preventing unfair market activities, the upcoming bill aims to provide clearer rules for the industry.

Authorities have previously indicated that the Digital Asset Basic Act would cover the legal definition of digital assets and comprehensive rules governing issuance and distribution. The draft is also expected to introduce a licensing regime for crypto businesses, shifting from the current notification system.

A more contested element of the bill is a proposed cap on ownership stakes held by major shareholders of crypto exchanges, widely reported to be in the range of 15% to 20%, to curb concentration risk. The measure has drawn strong opposition from the industry, with critics arguing that it would undermine free-market principles and property rights.

After the FSC releases the draft, it is expected to be merged with proposals from lawmakers and proceed to the National Assembly for further review and discussion.

​​Meanwhile, stablecoins are another major focus of the legislation. This follows South Korean President Lee Jae-myung calling for a local currency-based stablecoin market to protect the nation's monetary sovereignty in the digital age.

The government draft is expected to stipulate a bank-centered consortium model for issuing Korean won-pegged stablecoins, where banks would hold more than 50% in the consortium.

The country's central bank has pushed for this bank-first structure, having previously expressed concerns that unchecked stablecoin issuance could undermine monetary stability. This has also drawn backlash from local industry players who argued that setting this rule would deter innovation.

Other provisions in the bill are expected to further clarify different types of businesses, governance and internal controls of crypto projects, and establish conduct standards comparable to those for traditional financial companies. It would also further strengthen user protection requirements, including rules on asset segregation and operational safety.

#4964. Chainflip confirms $12M hack, offers attacker 10% bounty

Chainflip offered the attacker a 10% bounty to return 90% of the stolen funds by Nov. 23, promising to treat the return as a white-hat recovery and withdraw law enforcement complaints.

Cross-chain swap protocol Chainflip confirmed that an attacker stole about $12 million in Bitcoin, Ether and stablecoins from its vaults on Saturday, expanding the initially reported $4.86 million loss.

In a statement addressed to the attacker, Chainflip Labs said 122.86 Bitcoin (BTC), 520.22 Ether (ETH), 3.25 million USDC and 758,141 USDT were stolen in the Saturday incident.

The company offered the attacker a 10% bounty to return the remaining 90% of stolen assets by 18:38 UTC on Nov. 23. Chainflip said it would treat the return as a white-hat recovery and withdraw its reports and complaints to law enforcement if the funds were returned before the deadline.

According to CoinGecko data, Chainflip’s FLIP token plunged 42.9% over the past 24 hours.

Chainflip said it had traced preparations for the attack to Tornado Cash funding on Nov. 11 and a validator account registered on Friday.

The company said it had identified the mechanism behind the cryptographic key exposure and taken steps to prevent similar attacks. It also said it obtained identifying information linked to the attacker that could assist law enforcement.

“We hold identifying information on the validator and servers used, your addresses are flagged across every major analytics firm, and every Tornado Cash withdrawal is being watched,” Chainflip said.

#4963. Nvidia Soars as Huang Returns, Lifting Stocks and Crypto Shares

Nvidia shares jumped about 35% on Monday after the chipmaker reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, restoring roughly $1 trillion in market value at the open. The stock traded near $169.20 at 10:41 a.m. ET, up from Friday’s close of $125.53, and Wall Street rallied with it.

The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back, effective immediately, after what it called a series of discussions and meetings. It said it received input from “senior levels of the United States government” and is confident his return “poses no national security risk.” President Donald Trump had urged the move.

Several items remain open. An independent board committee will finish its investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, and Huang said he will cooperate. Nvidia also formed a national security and export control committee and is searching for a chief compliance officer.

Huang resigned on Nov. 11, days after admitting an affair with a woman U.S. officials believe is linked to Chinese intelligence. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress became interim CEO and Harvey Jones became board chair. Nvidia had said it was searching for a permanent successor.

The stock slid for seven straight weeks, the longest such streak since 2008. On Friday it plunged 14% after Reuters reported that the SEC is examining the company’s accounting practices. Reuters noted that investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing. Huang’s return reverses most of the losses since his affair became public.

The selloff came even after Nvidia reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Nov. 17. For weeks, the board had said it was not considering bringing Huang back, which makes Monday’s announcement a sharp turn for the world’s most closely watched chipmaker.

The Nasdaq Composite rose about 7.4% to near 24,300 at 10:41 a.m. ET, and the S&P 500 gained about 5.4% to near 7,280. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed about 3.3%, or more than 1,500 points, to near 49,700. The S&P 500 had fallen seven straight days.

Chip stocks followed Nvidia higher. Micron (MU) rose about 21% and Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) gained about 16%, while Intel (INTC) added about 15%. AMD rose about 9% and Broadcom (AVGO) was up about 3%.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned on Sunday that the Fed may be making a “policy mistake” if it overtightens. The central bank meets Dec. 8-9, and a quarter-point increase remains the base case.

The bitcoin price climbed to a Monday high near $64,500, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data, and was near $63,000 at 10:41 a.m. ET. That is about $8,000 above the weekend low of $55,106, hit at roughly 1:17 a.m. ET on Saturday. Bitcoin had slid with stocks on Friday.

Crypto-linked stocks jumped. Coinbase (COIN) rose about 9% to near $111, Robinhood (HOOD) gained about 11% and Circle (CRCL) added about 11%. Strategy (MSTR) climbed about 13% to near $88 after it disclosed a purchase of 457 bitcoin last week at an average of about $64,898, lifting its holdings to 851,305 BTC.

The rebound follows a rough stretch for bitcoin. It finished last week down about 6%, its seventh straight red weekly candle, and spot bitcoin ETFs shed about $1.79 billion, their fourth straight week of net outflows. Bitcoin has traded closely with technology stocks during the selloff.

Miners posted the biggest gains. IREN soared about 31%, while CleanSpark (CLSK) rose about 17% and MARA gained about 16%. Core Scientific (CORZ) added about 14% and Riot Platforms (RIOT) gained about 10%.

Bitcoin treasury companies also rallied. Strive (ASST) rose about 16%, Nakamoto (NAKA) gained about 6% and Twenty One Capital (XXI) added about 10%.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $63,000.

#4962. Inkling 2 Mini got 20 questions right but failed 4 out of 5 tests that required deeper thinking

Inkling 2 Mini’s repeated queries on a hidden-pattern test spotlight the need for tighter limits as local AI agents reach Macs.

In a hosted test published by Plotly on Nov. 21, the AI model Inkling 2 Mini got all 20 routine data questions right.

On one question about a hidden pattern, it made 585 queries over about 48 minutes and repeated the same few queries dozens of times, but it still missed the pattern.

In Plotly’s benchmark, Inkling 2 Mini scored 36 of 43 overall and found one of five hidden patterns. Plotly found that on the hidden-pattern questions, the model often added up the biggest totals and stopped.

Plotly ran the model through its own analytics software, Plotly Studio Embedded, using a version hosted by Prime Intellect and accessed through OpenRouter. It reported one scored sample per model, combining results with reruns of 16 Inkling 2 Mini questions that encountered a provider outage.

One scored sample using hosted inference.

On hidden-pattern questions, the model often stopped at overall totals before isolating the local signal.

The test leaves open how often the query loop would recur.

Each square represents one question in Plotly’s published results. Filled squares mark correct answers. The callout reports query count and approximate elapsed time for one failed question.

The test leaves open how often the query loop would recur.

Thinking Machines Lab released the downloadable weights on Nov. 20 under the Apache 2.0 license. Its model card lists support for Apple silicon Macs with at least 32 GB of memory.

The card lists a context window of up to 1 million tokens, which measures how much information the model can handle at once. How much of that window is usable on a particular Mac depends on the memory needed to process the request.

In the Nov. 22 release notes for oMLX 0.8.3, the Mac software’s maintainers reported about 20% faster prompt processing and 10% to 13% faster generation than in 0.8.2 for a reduced-precision build on an M5 Max.

The update also lets oMLX refuse prompts on a 32 GB Mac when it estimates they would exceed the memory budget.

In a Nov. 23 follow-up, an oMLX issue reporter said prompts of about 43,000 and 57,000 tokens were completed on one 32 GB M5 MacBook Pro using the updated software and a reduced-precision build. Reported memory use peaked at 23 GB and 24 GB, respectively.

Once a request fits, a separate limit can stop an agent from spending more turns on the same few queries.

Thinking Machines Lab says it saw the model repeatedly check its work without making progress in internal tests. The lab recommends caps on generated tokens and on the number of turns an agent can take.

In a statement on Sunday, Cuy Sheffield, Head of Visa Crypto Labs, said users can connect the wallet, add a Visa card on file, and use that credential to verify their agent and register it in Visa's Agent Directory. The wallet is built on Tempo using the Machine Payments Protocol.

Users can earn rewards when agents complete various tasks, such as paid surveys, music composition, market research, and gaming, according to the statement. Taskmarket, one of the platforms Visa is integrating with, allows buyers to post tasks and pay agents in OUSD or USDC on Tempo and Base if their submissions are accepted. Its website showed more than 25 open tasks for verified agents on Monday, with rewards ranging from 10 to 50 OUSD.

Sheffield said the product is intended to help users expand their productive capacity, and not replace them entirely.

"Rather than agents replacing individuals, we believe they extend an individual’s productive capacity to turn their thoughts and ideas into tangible insights and outputs that can create value in the global economy," he wrote.

The launch expands Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol and Agent Directory beyond their earlier applications in e-commerce and business payments, according to the statement.

Visa launched the protocol last October as a tool to help merchants establish whether an AI agent was authorized to transact on behalf of a person or business. Cloudflare, Akamai, and Billtrust were among the first companies to pilot the system.

Sheffield said Visa is extending the same verification tool to agent wallets and task marketplaces, starting with Visa CLI and Taskmarket. Expansion to other platforms is planned for later.

#4960. Coinbase Targets In-House Prediction Markets by First Half of 2027: Report

Coinbase Targets In-House Prediction Markets by First Half of 2027: Report

Coinbase is planning to launch its own prediction market contracts in the U.S. in the first half of 2027, as it looks to take more control of one of its fastest-growing businesses.

The exchange plans to offer the in-house event contracts to both retail and institutional customers, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter.

A Coinbase spokesperson told Bloomberg the company had "nothing new to announce today," and pointed to plans it set out in October to expand its prediction markets and improve their economics by building its own clearing and other infrastructure. The spokesperson did not address the timing of an in-house launch.

Coinbase rolled out prediction markets across the U.S. through a partnership with Kalshi, after unveiling the product alongside stock trading last year. Offering its own contracts would give Coinbase more say over which markets it lists, and let it keep more of the revenue from trades.

The exchange has been laying the groundwork for its pivot. In December 2025, it agreed to buy prediction markets startup The Clearing Company, and in September 2026 it received approval from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) for its own clearinghouse. Coinbase already runs a regulated derivatives exchange.

Prediction markets have become a bright spot for Coinbase as crypto trading slows. The business passed $200 million in annualized revenue in the third quarter, with daily traders up more than 60% from the previous quarter, and revenue growing 82% a quarter on average since launch, the company reported in October.

"Prediction markets are adding another revenue stream and are less correlated to crypto volatility," CFO Alesia Haas said at the time. On an analyst call the same day, Haas said Coinbase's new clearinghouse meant it "can launch our own contracts, and we can also then earn better economics," while continuing to offer contracts through partners such as Kalshi. Asked when, she said: "We have not shared a timeline."

The products have faced legal challenges from states that argue some event contracts amount to unlicensed gambling. Coinbase sued three states over their attempts to regulate prediction markets, and New York sued Coinbase and Gemini over their offerings in April.

Last week, a Louisiana judge temporarily barred more than 30 prediction market providers, including Coinbase's derivatives arm, from offering event contracts in the state, after Attorney General Liz Murrill sued them on November 12, Forbes reported. The CFTC has sued Louisiana in federal court to block the order, and a hearing on a longer injunction is set for November 30.

Decrypt's parent company, Dastan, operates its own prediction market, Decrypt Predict.

#4959. Solo Bitcoin Miner Wins $191,000 Block Reward With Just 11 TH/s

A solo miner running about 11 terahashes per second has mined Bitcoin block 977,057, collecting a reward of 3.1287 BTC, or about $191,000, on a machine that makes up roughly one-millionth of a percent of the network.

The block was found through the solo service at CKpool on Sunday, Nov. 22, at about 7:54 a.m. ET. The reward is the 3.125 BTC subsidy plus about 0.0037 BTC in transaction fees, and it was worth roughly $191,000 at bitcoin’s price when the block landed.

The block holds 584 transactions. Its coinbase transaction pays 3.0661 BTC to a single address and 0.0626 BTC, about 2% of the reward, to a second output. That split matches the service’s 2% fee, which means the miner’s take is a little over $186,000.

Con Kolivas, the developer behind CKpool, congratulated the miner on X, whose address he abbreviated as bc1q~zy9j. It matches the end of the address that received the payout. Kolivas called it the 323rd block found on the service and “yet another lucky one.”

He said the miner had only about 11.1 TH/s of hashrate on a 3.47 TH worker. “A miner of this size has about a one in 1650 chance of solving a block in a year,” Kolivas wrote.

The block was tagged to Solo CK on the mempool.space block explorer, and its coinbase carries the pool’s signature. CKpool describes itself as a service that lets miners go after full solo blocks without running their own node, since you cannot mine directly to a Bitcoin Core node.

Solo CK has found five blocks since Nov. 6, according to the explorer’s pool page. The most recent before this one was block 976,642 on Nov. 19, followed by blocks on Nov. 11, Nov. 7 and Nov. 6. Each paid between 3.13 and 3.15 BTC.

Earlier this year, a different solo miner won block 943,411 on the same service on April 2, for about 3.139 BTC. In October, a FutureBit Apollo solo miner found block 973,262 and earned 3.154 BTC.

Those wins are the exception. Most of the network’s hashrate sits in large pools and industrial operations that split rewards across many miners, which is how they smooth out the luck. A single small machine can run for years without finding anything, and a lucky block can show up on day one. Miners on the service get nothing unless they find a block, and then they keep the full reward minus the 2% fee.

Bitcoin’s network hashrate was about 1.04 zettahashes per second, or roughly 1,043 exahashes, on a three-day average Monday. At 11.1 TH/s, the winning miner contributes about 0.000001% of that total, which fits Kolivas’s odds. One in 1,650 works out to a chance of about 0.06% over a full year of mining.

Mining difficulty is about 134.8 trillion. The last adjustment cut it by about 9.1%, and the next one, expected around Nov. 26, is estimated to raise it by about 9.2%, according to mempool.space. Difficulty resets every 2,016 blocks to keep blocks arriving about every 10 minutes.

Mining conditions have been tough. Bitcoin plunged to about $55,100 over the weekend before rebounding to near $64,000 on Monday morning, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro. Lower prices cut the dollar value of every block, whether it goes to an industrial miner or a hobbyist running a small solo rig.

The subsidy is fixed at 3.125 BTC until the next halving, so what the solo winner earns depends on fees and the market. A 3.1287 BTC block was worth about $196,000 at Monday’s price near $62,700, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $62,700.

#4958. South Korean exchanges halt CYBER transfers amid suspected bridge exploit

Cyber reported unexpected minting of CYBER tokens on Solana, followed by tokens moving out of its Ethereum bridge lockbox, prompting an investigation.

South Korean crypto exchanges Upbit and Bithumb suspended deposits and withdrawals of CYBER after the project reported suspicious activity involving its cross-chain bridge.

On Sunday, Bithumb announced it would suspend deposits and withdrawals because of suspected security issues. The exchange said trading will continue, while transfers would resume once network stability was assured. Upbit also announced a temporary suspension of CYBER deposits and withdrawals.

On Saturday, Cyber said it detected unexpected minting of CYBER tokens on Solana, followed by a transfer of tokens out of its bridge’s Ethereum lockbox.

Cyber, formerly CyberConnect, operates an Ethereum layer-2 network designed for social applications.

The project said it was investigating the incident and assessing which assets and bridge routes were affected. It advised users to avoid using the bridge or depositing CYBER to exchanges while the investigation continues.

The suspensions come days after South Korea’s Financial Services Commission announced plans to allow exchanges to halt deposits and withdrawals when hacking is suspected, rather than waiting for a confirmed breach.

Earlier in November, South Korean exchange GOPAX also suspended trading, deposits and standard withdrawals after receiving a hacking threat, despite saying no breach had occurred.

LendingUSA has partnered with Cross River Bank to launch a bitcoin-secured lending program, allowing eligible borrowers to take out loans of $10,000 to $250,000 against their bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) holdings without selling them.

#4956. Bitcoin ETFs Shed $582M in a Day as BTC Drops Below $62K

Bitcoin ETFs Shed $582M in a Day as BTC Drops Below $62K

Bitcoin slid below $62,000 on Friday, extending a weeklong sell-off as investors pulled money from spot Bitcoin ETFs and braced for another interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve.

The leading cryptocurrency was trading at around $61,780, down 2.8% over the past day and 10% over the past week, after touching a 24-hour low of $61,273—its lowest level since early July—according to CoinGecko data. It has fallen more than $2,000 since struggling to hold $64,000 earlier this week, and has also formed a so-called death cross, a bearish chart pattern.

The drop triggered $727 million in liquidations across crypto markets over the past 24 hours, about 86% of which were long positions betting on higher prices, according to CoinGlass. Bitcoin accounted for just under $202 million of the total, with more than 151,000 traders liquidated.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $582.2 million in net outflows on Thursday, their largest single-day outflow since October 30, according to SoSoValue data. The funds have lost more than $1.1 billion so far this week and almost $3.5 billion in November, while their total net assets have fallen to $76.6 billion.

"Within crypto, the most telling sign is this month's outflow from spot Bitcoin ETFs, which suggests investors are choosing to stay on the sidelines for now," Neil Steinhardt, head of Nexo U.S., told Decrypt.

Treasury yields above 5% and expectations that the Fed will raise rates in December have weighed on assets that don't pay interest, including Bitcoin and gold, Steinhardt said. "Because the pressure appears tied to the rate backdrop, and that backdrop has shifted before, a turn in yields or the dollar would likely be the first signal that appetite is returning," he added, pointing to the December 4 jobs report and the Fed's December 9 meeting as the next checkpoints.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller has called for a larger, half-point increase at that meeting, unless policymakers signal another rise in January. Traders are betting on a smaller move: CME FedWatch puts the odds of a quarter-point hike on December 9 at 99.2%, with the chance of a half-point increase falling to almost zero from more than 9% on Thursday morning.

The decline has left the average Bitcoin holder only just in profit. Bitcoin is still trading above its realized price, the average price at which every coin on the network last moved, but the margin is thin, onchain analytics firm Glassnode tweeted on Friday. A break below would put holders in loss for the first time since early 2023, it said.

The average Bitcoin holder is still in profit.

bitcoin:native trades above its realized price, the average cost of every coin on the network. The margin is thin: MVRV sits just above 1.

A break below would put holders in loss for the first time since early 2023. pic.twitter.com/rPOTbZS1NF

— glassnode (@glassnode) November 20, 2026

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill sees the slide as part of a longer downturn. "I see this as a continuation of the existing bear market rather than the start of another," he said in a note published on Thursday, pointing to selling by large holders since late 2025, expectations of higher rates and weakness in tech stocks.

CoinShares' base case is for Bitcoin to trade between $60,000 and $90,000 through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives the Fed room to ease, Butterfill said.

#4951. ‘The dots aren’t done,’ Michael Saylor says as Strategy buys another 457 BTC for $30 million

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Strategy acquired another 457 BTC for approximately $29.6 million last week, with its total holdings now at 851,305 BTC.

Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) treasury company Strategy Strategy, Inc. (MSTR) bought another 457 BTC for $29.6 million at an average price of $64,898 per bitcoin between Nov. 16 and Nov. 22, according to a Monday filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The acquisitions increase Strategy's total bitcoin holdings to 851,305 BTC, bought for a total cost of approximately $64.2 billion at an average price of $75,446 per bitcoin, according to the filing. For perspective, that's equivalent to more than 4% of bitcoin's maximum supply cap, but reflects around $12 billion in paper losses at current prices.

The purchases were made using proceeds from at-the-market sales of its Class A common stock, MSTR. Strategy sold 1,925,676 MSTR shares for approximately $176.7 million last week. Approximately $17.9 billion worth of MSTR shares remain available under the ATM program, according to the filing.

Strategy also repurchased 2,183,747 STRC preferred shares between Nov. 16 and Nov. 22 for $211.8 million, using proceeds from its MSTR sales USD Cash reserve. The firm also used $17.6 million from its USD Reserve to pay for dividends on its preferred stocks.

On Friday, during the company's investor Q&A livestream, Strategy co-founder and Executive Chairman Michael Saylor said "natural, organic" demand for the company's STRC preferred stock at its current 12% dividend rate is likely between $5 billion and $7.5 billion.

Saylor described the current environment as a credit-market contraction, adding that the company is responding by reducing the amount of STRC outstanding until it reaches an equilibrium level that the market will support at the existing dividend rate. President and CEO Phong Le said the company has bought back about $3 billion of the preferred stock at prices between $95 and $99, below the $100 issuance price level.

As of Nov. 22, Strategy's USD Reserve and USD Cash balances stood at $3.73 billion and $1.09 billion, respectively, the firm said in the filing, after its board of directors authorized management to reallocate up to $1.0 billion from the USD Reserve to USD Cash.

Bitcoin fell another 6.3% last week, continuing a seven-week slump that saw the largest cryptocurrency drop to its lowest level since September 2024 over the weekend, wicking as low as $55,000 at one point. Bitcoin is currently trading for around $61,400 on Monday.

Despite the continued slide, Saylor posted yet another bitcoin acquisition tracker chart on Sunday stating, "The dots aren't done," indicating the potential acquisition announcement ahead of time.

MSTR fell 30.6% last week, closing on Friday at $77.80, its lowest level since February 2024, according to The Block's Strategy price page.
